catalog_quote: The Pearic word seems to have the same canonic shape as the word in most other Mon-Khmer languages. It consists of a single stressed syllable which may be preceded by a weakly stressed pre-syllable. The formulae below show the various components of the main syllable (MS) and the pre-syllable (PS). MS ⟶ C1 (C2) V1 (F1) PS ⟶ C3 (C4) V2 (F2) There are certain limitations on the membership in each one of these components. C1, which represents any consonant that can occur initially at the beginning of a stressed syllable, can be any consonant; ... C3 is any consonant which can occur as the initial consonant in a presyllable, and is apparently limited to /p t k s l/, and C4 is limited to /r/ and /l/. V1 represents any vowel or vowel cluster which can occur as the nucleus of a stressed syllable. Short vowels are not found in open syllables. V2, the vowel nucleus of the presyllable, is a neutra…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pearic words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables: the single main (final) syllable carries the stress; an optional presyllable before it is only weakly stressed and has a reduced neutral vowel. I.e. word stress is fixed on the final (main) syllable of the phonological word. This is stated for the Pearic branch as a whole (Headley's comparison explicitly includes Suoi of Kompong Speu, from Baradat's 1941 manuscript), not from first-hand Suoy phonetics.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Presyllable described as 'weakly stressed'; no further statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress; notes only that the presyllable is lost entirely in some Chong dialects of Thailand. Baradat 1941 (the underlying Suoi source) adds that the dialects are 'monotoniques' (no lexical tone).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (native) phonological word = main syllable plus optional presyllable; nothing said about polysyllabic Khmer loans, compounds or phrase-level prominence. Genus-level generalisation in a comparative reconstruction paper whose Suoy data are second-hand written transcriptions (Baradat 1941, Pannetier ms).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is a branch-level generalisation about 'the Pearic word' (all Pearic dialects, Headley's Map 1 no. 9 = Suoi of Kompong Speu), not a description of Suoy in particular; Headley's Suoi data are Baradat's 1941 written transcriptions. No first-hand phonological description of Suoy [syo] exists in Glottolog, OLAC or the SEAlang Pearic project. The closest first-hand sibling statement is for Sa'och/Chung (saoc1239, same 'Southern Chong' node): Isara 2007 pp. 52-53, unstressed CV minor syllable + stressed major syllable. Note also the name trap flagged by Ferlus 2011: 'Suay/Suoy' is also used for Katuic Kuy groups (e.g. kuyy1240) -- not this language.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 pp. 429/431: 'The Pearic word.. consists of a single stressed syllable which may be preceded by a weakly stressed pre-syllable'; MS = C1(C2)V1(F1), PS = C3(C4)V2(F2); presyllable vowel a neutral /e/; 'The presyllable is reduced to zero in some of the Chong dialects of Thailand.' Branch-level statement; Map 1 (p. 430) and the classification include '9 Suoi of Kompong Speu' (data from Baradat 1941 ms). Nothing Suoy-specific on stress.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Considerations generales' (typescript pp. ~5-9): 'Les dialectes samre sont monotoniques' (non-tonal, contra Rousseau's 'polytonique'); pronunciation 'plus gutturale.. des voyelles plus appuyees, comme martelees'; transcription conventions (vowel echo 'the-e', etc.). No statement on where the accent falls. Remaining ~230 pp. are word lists (not scanned). The only primary source containing Suoi/Suoy language data.
